SSA capitulates: Media, civil society win access to Dlomo state capture trial

Kyle Cowan
Comments
Bookmark
Add as a preferred source on Google
0:00
Subscribers can listen to this article
Former SSA investigator Patrick Mshothola (left) and Thulani Dlomo (right) were arrested on graft charges by the Investigating Directorate Against Corruption. Now the media and civil society groups have won access to their criminal trial, overturning a court order that it be held in secret.
Supplied/Thulani Dlomo Foundation
  • The SSA backed down and agreed to a court order granting media access to Dlomo’s trial, reversing the judge’s earlier blanket ban.
  • The media will receive some evidentiary documents in full; the rest will be disclosed only in redacted form, with the right to further challenges to access reserved.
  • The trial continues today before Judge Munzhelele, with Dlomo and Mshotola facing fraud, forgery and theft charges over R12 million in SSA cash.
  • For secure, anonymous communication with News24’s investigations team, click here.

Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:51
Instaread

The State Security Agency has capitulated and agreed to a court order allowing media access to the trial of Thulani Dlomo and Patrick Mshotola.

On Thursday, Judge Mashudu Munzhelele in the Gauteng High Court in Pretoria handed down an order that varied her previous ruling, which had prevented the public and media from attending proceedings.

The new order will also grant the media access to some of the evidentiary documents that form the basis of the charges, while the remainder will be disclosed only in redacted form.

The media application was brought by Media24, Daily Maverick, the amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism, and the civil society organisation the Campaign for Free Expression (CFE). The Mail and Guardian brought a separate legal attack.

ADVERTISEMENT

READ | ‘Unlawful, unconstitutional’: Media, civil society in court over closed trial of Zuma’s spy

The effect of Thursday’s order is that the media will now be allowed to attend the trial, in which Dlomo and Mshotola are accused of fraud, forgery, and theft for misappropriating R12 million in SSA funds, subject to certain conditions.

The order sets out that the SSA will immediately hand over documents it had agreed could be shared, including a contract between the SSA and a company named Karolo Investments and invoices.

“The applicants reserve their rights to seek access to the remainder of the documents through any appropriate litigation process,” the order reads.

ADVERTISEMENT

Court battle

On Wednesday, the SSA brought an application before the court to have the entire case held behind closed doors, citing unspecified concerns that public and media access would threaten national security.

Acting SSA director-general James Ramabulana argued in court papers that the agency fears that trade secrets and operational matters could become public knowledge.

Ramabulana held that his application is to protect the SSA’s sources, methods, techniques and operations while the trial “proceeds undisturbed”.

His affidavit reads:

I have no interest in shielding them [Dlomo, Mshotola] from accountability. I have an obligation to protect the lives of those who protect the country from outside threats. I seek to protect the identities of former and serving members, sources, operational infrastructure, intelligence methods, techniques, privileged intelligence cooperation agreements from unauthorised disclosure.

“I do not have the authority to stop the accused from testifying in their trial. I have no control [over] what the accused may say in their testimony in Court. They may well divulge all of the confidential and classified information, as well as the SSA operational intelligence-gathering methods and sources. I have no way to stop them,” Ramabulana added.

After protracted negotiations between the media and civil society applications and the SSA, the latter backtracked.

The trial continues before Munzhelele on Thursday, with News24 now in attendance.
